name: The Paradox of Fiction
aliases: The paradox of emotional response to fiction
statement: How can we feel real emotions for characters we know do not exist?
statementAccent: for characters we know do not exist
meaning: The paradox of fiction is the puzzle of how we can have genuine emotional responses toward characters, objects, and events we know to be fictional. We feel pity for Anna Karenina, fear while watching a horror film, and grief at a character's death, yet we know these characters and events are not real, and we do not act as we would if they were, calling the police or fleeing the cinema. The puzzle is standardly presented as an inconsistent triad, three individually plausible but jointly incompatible claims, whose modern discussion was launched by Colin Radford's 1975 paper How Can We Be Moved by the Fate of Anna Karenina?. The first claim is that we do in fact have emotional responses to characters and situations we know to be fictional. The second is that emotions of this kind require, or presuppose, that we believe the objects of the emotion actually exist or that the situations are real, an existence-belief condition on emotion. The third is that we do not believe fictional characters and situations exist, since we know them to be fictional. All three cannot be true together. Radford himself concluded that our responses are in a way incoherent or irrational. The main solutions each reject one leg of the triad: the illusion theory, the thought theory of Lamarque and Carroll, and Kendall Walton's pretend or make-believe theory.
mechanism: The paradox is generated by the collision of three claims each of which is hard to deny. We plainly do respond emotionally to fiction, weeping, trembling, and rejoicing at what happens to characters we care about. It seems equally plain that ordinary emotions like fear and pity involve beliefs about their objects, that to fear something is to believe it dangerous and real, and to pity someone is to believe they exist and suffer. And it is certain that, as competent consumers of fiction, we do not believe the characters and events are real. Since these cannot all hold, a solution must reject one. The illusion or suspension-of-disbelief theory rejects the third claim, proposing that while absorbed in the fiction we momentarily believe, or half-believe, or forget, that it is unreal; most philosophers reject this, since we do not in fact lose our knowledge that the film is fiction, as our failure to intervene shows. The thought theory, associated with Peter Lamarque and Noel Carroll, rejects the second claim, arguing that emotions can be generated by merely entertaining or vividly imagining a thought or mental representation, without any belief that its object exists, so that genuine emotion does not require existence-belief and our responses to fiction are genuine emotions directed at contents we merely entertain. Kendall Walton's pretend or make-believe theory, in his 1978 paper Fearing Fictions, rejects the first claim, arguing that we do not literally fear or pity; rather, engaging with fiction is a game of make-believe in which we have quasi-emotions, and it is fictionally true that we fear, so our states are not ordinary emotions of the everyday kind.

examples.text: We respond to fiction, emotions require belief in the object's existence, and we know fiction is not real, three claims that clash.
Lamarque and Carroll hold that vividly entertaining a thought can generate genuine emotion without belief in its object's existence.
Walton argued we do not literally fear fictions but have quasi-fear within a game of make-believe, where it is fictional that we fear.

variants.name: Solutions by rejected premise
variants.text: The illusion theory rejects our knowing it is fiction, the thought theory the existence-belief condition, and the pretend theory that we feel real emotion.

variants.name: Radford's irrationalism
variants.text: Radford's own conclusion that our emotional responses to fiction are incoherent or irrational, keeping all three claims.

whyItMatters: The paradox of fiction is a central problem in the philosophy of emotion and of fiction, because it exposes a tension in something we do constantly and value deeply: responding emotionally to stories, films, plays, and novels. Fiction moves us, often more powerfully than much of real life, yet on reflection it is puzzling that we should be moved at all by what we know does not exist, and the paradox forces us to say what emotions really are, whether they require beliefs about the existence of their objects, and how imagination engages the feelings. The solutions map the main options in the theory of emotion: the thought theory loosens the tie between emotion and belief, while Walton's make-believe theory reconceives our engagement with fiction as a game of imagination generating quasi-emotions, an account with wide influence on the philosophy of representation. The problem connects to empathy, to imaginative immersion, and to the larger question of why fiction matters and how it can educate and move us. Launched by Radford's provocation about Anna Karenina, it has generated decades of debate.

working.text: observe that we genuinely feel pity, fear, or grief toward fictional characters and events.
note that ordinary emotions seem to require believing their objects exist, which we do not believe of fiction.
resolve the clash by denying illusion, the existence-belief condition, or that the responses are ordinary emotions.

limits: The paradox of fiction remains unresolved, with each solution facing objections. The illusion theory is widely rejected, since we do not really lose our knowledge that the fiction is fiction, as our lack of action shows. The thought theory, on which entertaining a vivid thought suffices for genuine emotion, is challenged to explain why some thoughts move us and others do not, and whether emotions so generated are really the same kind as ordinary belief-based emotions. Walton's make-believe theory, on which we feel only quasi-emotions, is criticized for denying the evident phenomenological reality of the feelings, which seem to be real fear and real pity, not merely pretended ones. There is also debate about whether the second premise, that emotion requires existence-belief, was ever as compelling as the paradox assumes. Some attributions and details reward care: Radford's 1975 paper was a symposium co-authored with Michael Weston, Walton's Fearing Fictions dates to 1978, and there is no standalone Stanford Encyclopedia entry under this title, the topic being covered in the Internet Encyclopedia and under imagination.
misreadings: The paradox of fiction is not the claim that our responses to fiction are fake or shallow; the puzzle is precisely that they seem genuine and strong despite our knowing the object is unreal. It does not assume we are fooled into believing the fiction is real, which the illusion theory proposes but most reject. And rejecting the second premise, that emotion requires existence-belief, is one live solution rather than a concession that there is no puzzle, so treating our responses as insincere, as resting on illusion, or as obviously requiring existence-belief, misreads the paradox.
origin: The puzzle, given modern form by Colin Radford's 1975 paper on Anna Karenina, of how we can have genuine emotional responses to characters and events we know to be fictional, framed as an inconsistent triad.

sources.text: The Paradox of Fiction, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the paradox as an inconsistent triad, Radford's 1975 paper and his conclusion that the responses are irrational, and the illusion, thought, and pretend or make-believe solutions of the illusion theorists, Lamarque and Carroll, and Walton.

Imagination, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the role of imagination in emotional engagement with fiction, Walton's make-believe theory and quasi-emotions, and the relation of imagining to belief and feeling.
